tasks.short: Write and sign the network disaster recovery plan

steps.what: Send system list and recovery targets
Check targets against the live inventory

loop.output: gap list of missing or conflicting targets
loop.check: Each gap names a system id that exists on the inventory
loop.stop: One pass, then the architect finishes any row with no system id
loop.why_not_simpler: Free-text notes do not match inventory ids by a fixed rule

steps.what: Draft the recovery plan from the template

loop.input: signed target fields and template sections
loop.output: plan draft with each number tagged to a field
loop.check: Every recovery number equals the submitted field
loop.stop: Leave a blank and stop that section if a number has no field
loop.why_not_simpler: Dependency prose varies by site and a fixed mail-merge cannot write it

steps.what: Sign the plan version in review
File the signed plan and test date
Confirm the next tabletop test slot

tasks.design: Service owners submit system id, recovery-point hours, recovery-time hours, owner and dependencies on a {WORKFLOW} form. A bounded draft fills the plan template in {DOCS}, and every number must match a submitted field. The network architect signs one version, and only that version is filed with a test date on the {CALENDAR}.
tasks.previous_blocker: Plans were recopied from old documents, and the recovery numbers lived in mail, so a draft would have repeated stale targets.
tasks.enabler_now: The inventory and the target form can share one system id, so each number in the draft can be checked against a field.
tasks.still_hard: Deciding which systems may stay down, and for how long, is still a business call.
tasks.human_edge: The architect decides which dependencies are real and which recovery time the business can accept.

ambition.what: Re-sign the recovery plan after each major site change, not only at the yearly review

tasks.altitude: The week moves from rewriting sections to resolving target conflicts and signing. The architect can refuse a plan whose numbers do not match the form.

reach.task: Check backups against signed recovery targets
reach.learn: Which targets are signed and which rows are still blank

evidence.claim: In a mid-size firm this task is mostly a document plus a review, and the hard part is the recovery targets rather than the formatting.
Digest [S3] says a document product can fill metadata from a prompt, and the vendor warns the fill can be wrong, so a person still checks the numbers.
Digest [S16] and [S17] say Dutch cyber law has been in force since 15 August 2026 and includes a duty of care; sector and size decide whether a firm is in scope.

assumptions: Focal role is the network architect. The task ends when a signed plan version is filed. Running the failover test is a later task.

Input contract: system id, recovery-point hours, recovery-time hours, business owner, dependency system ids, last test date. Producer is the service owner. If the form is empty the architect types the same fields from mail and marks the row manual.
Use the document store's own templates and approval flow before custom code. Template upkeep is counted in incremental hours, not assumed to be zero.
unknowns: Whether this firm is in scope of the Dutch cyber duty of care.
Which system is the inventory of record.
Who may sign when the architect is absent.
research_questions: How often do signed targets differ from the last test result?
Which sites have no named business owner?

already_counted.description: Architect edits weak dependency sections in the draft
Architect resolves conflicting targets in the sign-off

incremental.description: Update the plan template when a new site type appears
Service owners correct stale targets the form rejects

approvals.approved_version: recovery plan version signed in this review
the same signed recovery plan version

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes half the sites still arrive as free-text mail, so the architect retypes targets. The high case assumes the form is used but every plan still has a full sign-off. The failover test itself is not treated as saved.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Recommend firewall, audit and probe measures

steps.what: Read firewall hits and probe results
Draft the rule or audit note

loop.input: finding rows and the recommendation template
loop.output: note that cites rule ids only
loop.check: Every cited rule id is on the finding list
loop.stop: Stop after one draft; drop any sentence with no rule id
loop.why_not_simpler: The narrative of why a rule should change is not a fixed lookup

steps.what: Decide which measures to recommend
Check the control gap
Apply only the signed firewall change

tasks.design: Probe and firewall logs land on a {BI} view filtered to new and expiring rules. A bounded note in {DOCS} drafts the recommendation from those rows only. The architect decides what to recommend, and a {OPS_SYSTEM} change runs only for the signed rule version.
tasks.previous_blocker: Evidence for a rule change was spread across consoles and meeting notes, so a draft could not show which finding it relied on.
tasks.enabler_now: Rule hits, probe results and expiry dates can be exported as rows with a rule id.
tasks.still_hard: Whether a risky rule stays open is a trade-off with the business, not a threshold.
tasks.human_edge: The architect accepts or rejects an exception and sets its expiry.

ambition.what: Review firewall exceptions every month instead of only at the yearly audit

tasks.altitude: Less time collecting screenshots, more time on exceptions. The architect can block a change that has no signed rule version.

reach.task: Retest a control the architect marked weak
reach.learn: Which findings the architect has already accepted and until when

evidence.claim: Digest [S7] and [S8] describe a managed detection service for mid-size firms that uses models to speed investigation, while the analysts still decide.
Digest [S13] reports an observational study of live security operations with shorter resolve times after a generative assistant versus matched peers. It was not a randomised trial.
Digest [S14] says a vendor pentest agent had 130 of about 1,060 reports resolved, and many of the rest were duplicates or informative, so probe output still needs a person.
Digest [S16] and [S18] say that for firms in scope, the Dutch cyber duty of care includes patching and supply-chain measures. Scope depends on sector and size.

assumptions: Focal role is the network architect. Applying a change on a production firewall is in this task only after a signed rule version.
Input contract: rule id, hit count, last-change date, owner, probe id, severity. Producer is the monitoring export. If the export lacks a rule id, the row stays on a manual list.
Native alerting and the existing change window are configured first. Logging of staff traffic stays limited to security events.
unknowns: Whether production rule changes are frozen outside a change window.
Who owns exceptions that belong to a supplier.
Whether this firm is in scope of the cyber duty of care.
research_questions: What share of firewall rules has no owner or no expiry?
How many probe findings were duplicates last quarter?

already_counted.description: Architect edits the recommendation before the decision

incremental.description: Keep the finding filters and note template aligned with new probe types
Analyst time on control comments is already in s4; extra retests sit here

approvals.approved_version: measure decision signed in this review

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes probe exports stay unstructured, so the architect still assembles the evidence by hand. The high case assumes rows are clean but every exception still gets a human decision. Pentest scope is not widened.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Choose and apply a fix for a network fault

steps.what: Open the failing path on the monitor
Draft two fixes from the runbook

loop.output: two fixes each citing one runbook id
loop.check: Each fix cites a runbook id for that symptom code
loop.stop: If no entry matches, return an empty note and stop
loop.why_not_simpler: Matching a new symptom phrase to a runbook needs reading, not a fixed table

steps.what: Choose the fix and the rollback
Apply the change on the network
Confirm the path works again

tasks.design: A {BI} view opens on the failing path from the {OPS_SYSTEM}. A bounded note drafts two candidate fixes from the runbook, each tied to a symptom code. The architect picks one and the rollback, then applies it. The user confirms the path. Uncoded faults stay on the manual queue.
tasks.previous_blocker: Fault notes were free text in mail and chat, so similar incidents did not line up with a runbook entry.
tasks.enabler_now: Monitoring can emit a path id and a symptom code that a runbook can key on.
tasks.still_hard: Novel faults and changes on live traffic still depend on the architect's call.
tasks.human_edge: The architect chooses the fix and decides when a live change is safe to roll back.
tasks.altitude: Known faults take less gathering. The architect keeps the right to apply or refuse a live change.

reach.task: Run the rollback the architect named
reach.learn: Which symptom codes already have a signed fix and which must wait

evidence.claim: Most network faults in a mid-size firm are diagnosed from monitors and then changed by hand. Only repeated, coded cases suit a runbook.
Digest [S7] and [S8] describe a managed detection service that speeds investigation for mid-size firms, while a person still decides what to do.
Digest [S28] reports a coding agent that deleted a production database despite instructions, so an unattended change on live network gear is out of scope.

assumptions: Focal role is the network architect. The task runs from a detected fault to a confirmed path or a stopped attempt.
Input contract: path id, symptom code, start time, affected site, last change id. Producer is the monitoring system. Faults without a symptom code skip the draft and go to the manual choice.
The prior on meetings is high. For this task the time is on the monitor, the runbook and the change itself. User confirmation stays a short check, not a meeting.
unknowns: Whether the architect or an operator is allowed to change production during the day.
Which devices expose a job interface versus a console only.
research_questions: What share of faults repeat a symptom code already in the runbook?
How often is the first fix rolled back?

already_counted.description: Architect reviews a weak draft before choosing
Hands-on change time remains with the architect

incremental.description: Add new symptom codes to the runbook after repeated faults

approvals.approved_version: fix and rollback chosen for this fault id

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes most faults have no symptom code, so the draft rarely fires and the architect still diagnoses by hand. The high case assumes coded faults draft cleanly but every live change and rollback stays manual. No unattended changes.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Run backups and approved folder or file changes

steps.what: Submit the folder or backup request
Sign this period's backup policy
Run the backups the policy names
Approve a deletion or a new share
Apply the approved share change
Handle a failed job or an odd path

tasks.design: Requesters submit a folder, restore or backup request on a {WORKFLOW} form with an owner and a system id. Scheduled backups run from a signed policy in the {OPS_SYSTEM}. Deletions and new shares run only after the architect signs that request version. Failed jobs stay on a {BI} list for a person.
tasks.previous_blocker: Requests arrived by mail and the backup success was checked by eye, so a job could not know which request was approved.
tasks.enabler_now: Backup products already run on a schedule. The missing piece is a signed policy version and a request id.
tasks.still_hard: A deletion of the wrong share is costly, and some appliances still have no job interface.
tasks.human_edge: The architect signs deletions and new shares, and stops a job that looks wrong.

ambition.what: Small-site staff can request a restore without waiting for a visit

tasks.altitude: The architect leaves scheduled backups alone and keeps the right to refuse a deletion. Failed jobs are the remaining queue.

reach.task: Rerun a failed backup the architect stopped
reach.learn: Which policy version is current and which failures are already accepted

evidence.claim: Scheduled backup jobs are already normal on network file services. The remaining human work is requests, deletions and failed jobs.
Digest [S22] says security logging must stay necessary and proportionate. A backup log should record job result and owner, not file contents.
Digest [S16] and [S18] say firms in scope of the Dutch cyber duty of care have continuity obligations. Whether this firm is in scope is a separate fact.

assumptions: Focal role is the network architect. The task covers file and backup changes on network storage, not desktop support.
Input contract: request type, system id, path, owner, ticket id. Producer is the requester. Requests with no owner or no system id are rejected by rule and not approved by hand.

The meeting-heavy time prior does not fit this task. Time today sits on the console and the request mailbox. Works-council consent applies if job logs are later used to watch staff, which this design does not do.
Appliances with no job interface stay manual. That is why the saved range sits well below the central case.
unknowns: Which storage still has no job interface.
Whether restores of personal folders need a privacy review.
Who may sign a deletion when the architect is away.
research_questions: What share of backup jobs failed last month?
How many deletions are requested in a typical week?

already_counted.description: Policy sign-off time stays with the architect
Deletion judgement stays with the architect
Failed-job review stays with the architect

incremental.description: Revise backup policy fields when a new storage type is added

approvals.approved_version: backup policy version for this period
the same signed backup policy version
share or deletion decision for this request id

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes many appliances have no job interface, so backups stay manual and only the request form is new. The high case assumes scheduled backups run, while every deletion and every failed job still takes architect time.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The architect stops rewriting recovery text and routine notes, and spends the week on target conflicts, change choices and failed jobs.
reach: Information security analysts can read the signed recovery targets instead of asking again.
Network operators take the filed test date and the backup policy as their queue.
skills_to_grow: Write recovery targets as fields a template can check.
State a firewall change as a reversible rule with an owner and an expiry.
Separate a standard backup job from a deletion that still needs a signature.
role.ambitious_version: Every new site opens with a signed recovery plan, a named backup policy and a short list of accepted firewall exceptions.
